newsitem.title: FALKLAND ISLANDS: Argentines say cemetery visit to Falklands success.
newsitem.headline: Argentines say cemetery visit to Falklands success.

text.p: Argentines who flew to the disputed Falklands to see the graves of relatives killed in the 1982 war said on Thursday the visit had been a success and the islanders treated them well.
"We want everyone in Argentina to know that we were well received and cared for by the islanders," said Hector Cisneros, President of the Argentine Dependent Families Commission.
"Nobody bothered us or protested at our presence and our sorrow was respected," he told reporters after the two-day visit by 15 relatives of the war dead.
Eight brothers, five mothers, one wife and one sister took the emotional trip to the islands 15 years after Argentina invaded and Britain sent a task force to dislodge its troops.
"The entire group is returning to Argentina feeling quite comforted for being in the islands because 15 years is a long time to wait and see the graves of our loved ones," Cisneros said.
Despite official rapprochement between Britain and Argentina, the Falklanders remain deeply mistrustful of a country that still lays claim to the islands, known in Latin America as the Malvinas.
Falklands councillors have called on the Argentine government to exhume its war dead, so far without success, fearing visits by mourning relatives.

British authorities have urged the Falklanders to take a more conciliatory approach in line with detente that brought renewed diplomatic ties in 1989, high-profile visits to Argentina by British royals and rapid expansion of trade links.
Cisneros said he preferred visits by smaller groups because they are "much more organised, manageable and orderly and far preferable to large groups."
Asked if the visit had been a success, he said: "Very good, very good."
The Darwin cemetery contains 234 bodies of which only 111 are identified. The rest of Argentina's war dead were lost at sea.
This week's trip -- another group of 15 will visit in February -- follows similar such visits in 1986, 1991 and 1995.
The repeated visits have angered Falklands councillors, who wanted a larger, one-off visit. They were also opposed to the families staying overnight and being lodged at Darwin.
